assets.topic: Coaching a Critical Incident: The Disruptive Label
assets.visual_frame_description: A sunny Friday afternoon in the Self Science classroom at the Nueva Learning Center. Rahman, tall with a shock of bushy black hair cut into a longish crew cut, faces Tucker, whose neatly combed blond hair and baggy blue "Be Responsible" T-shirt mark him as the group's official observer. Between them, on the table, lies the evaluation sheet with Rahman's name written under "Who is disruptive?" Their voices are rising into an aggressive staccato as the rest of the class clears away the Cooperation Squares puzzles.
assets.player_mission: You are Jo-An Varga, the teacher arriving at the boys' table at the height of the dispute. Coach both boys through the exchange so the conflict cools into a lesson instead of escalating, and make sure each boy is heard and understood before the class moves on.
key_concepts: In Self Science, spontaneous exchanges of heated feeling are treated as "critical incidents": moments when lessons already learned pay off and new ones can be taught most profitably.
Lessons applied in such electric moments last in students' memories, which is why teachers capitalize on them.
Karen Stone McCown's curriculum teaches that anger is almost always a secondary reaction and coaches children to look for what is underneath: hurt, jealousy, or being left out.

Conflict typically escalates from not communicating, making assumptions, and jumping to conclusions, and from sending a "hard" message in ways that make it tough for people to hear what you are saying.
Nueva teaches assertiveness - expressing feelings forthrightly in a way that will not spiral into aggression - from third grade on, as distinct from aggression or passivity.
Active listening is shown by facing the other person, making eye contact, and sending the silent cues that let a speaker know he is being heard.
Mastery in the emotional domain is especially difficult because skills must be acquired when people are usually least able to take in new information: when they are upset.

As Varga puts it, "Anyone, adult or fifth grader, needs some help being a self-observer when they're so upset" - heart pounding, hands sweaty, trying to listen clearly without screaming, blaming, or clamming up in defensiveness.
The observer's evaluation sheet, listing who took the lead, who was a clown, and who disrupted, was the unspoken source of the conflict: Tucker had written Rahman's name under "disruptive."
The goal of the conflict-resolution lessons is not to avoid conflict but to resolve disagreement and resentment before it spirals into an out-and-out fight.
Neither Tucker nor Rahman resorted to blaming, name-calling, a contemptuous "f you!", a fist fight, or stalking out of the room, thanks to lessons already in place.
The purpose of the day's postmortem is to dissect how the heated exchange and its cooling-down drew on conflict-resolution skills.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests emotional coaching at a critical incident: the teacher names the secondary emotion (hurt at being labeled "disruptive") beneath the surface anger and reframes the other boy's intent so both boys feel heard. Goleman reports that such electric moments, when lessons already learned pay off, are when new habits of response are taught most profitably and retained longest.

credibility.basis: Popular synthesis of affective research; EI construct scope debated

assets.scenario_setup: Right after the Cooperation Squares game, Rahman and Tucker are locked in a contentious argument over whether offering a puzzle piece counts as gesturing. Their volume is rising, and Rahman keeps glancing at Tucker's evaluation sheet, which lists his name under "Who is disruptive?" - the hidden source of his ire. You are the teacher at their table, with the goal of turning this electric moment into the day's most lasting lesson rather than shutting it down or letting it escalate.
dialogue: Rahman: "But offering a piece IS gesturing - you said no gesturing!"
Tucker: "You can too offer a piece - that's not gesturing." (emphatic, argumentative)
Rahman: "That is gesturing, and you know it." (vehement)
Varga (you): "This isn't a criticism - you cooperated very well - but Tucker, try to say what you mean in a tone of voice that doesn't sound so critical."
Tucker (calmer): "You can just put a piece where you think it goes, give someone what you think they need, without gesturing. Just offering."
Rahman (still angry): "You could have just gone like this" - he scratches his head to illustrate an innocent movement - "and he'd say 'No gesturing!'"
Varga (you, noticing Rahman eyeing the sheet): "He's feeling that you used a negative word - disruptive - about him. What did you mean?"
Tucker (conciliatory): "I didn't mean it was a bad kind of disruption."
Rahman: "That's a little farfetched, if you ask me."
choices: Tucker is trying to say that what could be considered disruptive could also be part of lightening things up during a frustrating time - and Rahman, I appreciate the way you're being assertive without attacking.
Rahman, stop overreacting. Tucker already said he didn't mean it that way. Drop it and help clean up the puzzles.
Tucker, you apologize right now for writing 'disruptive' on that sheet, and Rahman, you apologize for using that tone.
Both of you, that's enough raised voices. Report to the principal's office so this argument can be handled properly.
assets.theoretical_principle: Anger as a secondary reaction plus emotional coaching in critical incidents: name the feeling underneath the anger (hurt at the label), reframe the other's intent, and coach the tone of the message rather than adjudicating blame.
assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 0 names the hidden feeling - Rahman's hurt at being called disruptive - and reframes Tucker's intent as lightening things up, which is exactly the coaching Stone McCown describes: when we teach about anger, we look for what's underneath. Choice 1 dismisses Rahman's feeling as an overreaction, the "jumping to conclusions" that escalates conflict. Choice 2 forces apologies without addressing the hurt beneath, teaching role compliance rather than assertion and real listening. Choice 3 removes the conflict from the learning moment entirely, delegating the "electric moment" to authority instead of mining it for a lasting lesson.

assets.topic: Peer Mediation at the Cafeteria Door
assets.visual_frame_description: A busy lunch recess at a New York City public school. Near the cafeteria door, Darius and Miguel stand face to face, red-faced and shouting over a disputed handball call, while a ring of onlookers forms. Priya, an eleven-year-old trained peer mediator, arrives with a calm, unhurried manner and motions both boys to sit on the bench, her mediation ground rules humming behind her eyes.
assets.player_mission: You are Priya's co-mediator in the Resolving Conflict Creatively Program. Run the protocol: keep the boys calm, get each to state his position, make each paraphrase the other, and steer them toward a solution both sides can live with - before the dispute carries over into tomorrow.
key_concepts: The Resolving Conflict Creatively Program operates in several hundred New York City public schools and schools across the country.
Founder Linda Lantieri: "The program shows students that they have many choices for dealing with conflict besides passivity or aggression."
A key to the program's success is extending it to the playground and cafeteria, where tempers are more likely to explode.
Students can be trained as mediators starting in the latter years of elementary school, learning to handle fights, taunts, threats, and interracial incidents.
Mediators learn to phrase their statements so that both parties feel the mediator is impartial.
The protocol has each party calm down and state their position, then paraphrase what has been said so it is clear they have really heard.
Settlements are often formalized as signed agreements both sides can live with.
Former student mediator Angel Perez: "If something's done negative to me, I don't try to do the negative thing back - I try to solve the problem."

Lantieri holds that preventing violence cannot be separated from the full spectrum of emotional competence: knowing what you feel, handling impulse, naming an expanded range of feelings, and empathizing.
Evaluations of the program point with pride to increases in "caring among the kids" as well as drops in fights, put-downs, and name-calling.
One exercise asks students to think of a single realistic step, no matter how small, that might have helped settle a past conflict.
Lantieri: "Kids learn to stand up for their rights without resorting to violence. These are lifelong skills, not just for those most prone to violence."
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests peer mediation built on perspective-taking and impartial reframing: each party calms down, states a position, and paraphrases the other's, then brainstorms solutions both can live with, often sealed by a signed agreement. Goleman reports that the success of the Resolving Conflict Creatively Program depends on taking these tools to the playground and cafeteria, where tempers are most likely to explode.

credibility.basis: Popular synthesis of affective research; EI construct scope debated

assets.scenario_setup: The dispute: Miguel insists Darius called his ball out when it was clearly in; Darius claims Miguel shoved him after losing. The yard monitor called Priya in before it turned physical. If you leave them unresolved, retaliation is likely tomorrow; your goal is a settlement both boys accept as fair, with the hostility drained out of the exchange.
dialogue: Miguel: "He cheated and he knows it. I'm not playing with him ever again."
Darius: "You're just mad because you lost. You always make excuses."
Priya (you): "Okay, let's slow it down. Darius, can you say what happened, without any name-calling?"
Darius: "He called my ball out when it was clearly in. That's cheating, that's what it is."
Priya (you): "Miguel, can you repeat back in your own words what Darius just said?"
Miguel: "He thinks I called a ball out that he thinks was in. Fine, I heard him. But then he shoved me."
Priya (you): "Good - you both heard each other. Now for the shove: Miguel, what would feel fair to you about how that should be handled?"
Miguel: "An apology. And for the record, I did not call that ball out - or maybe I did by accident. I was looking at the fence."
Darius: "An apology, okay. And I shouldn't have shoved him."
choices: Excellent - that right there is the settlement. Turn to them: "Darius, is apologizing for the shove something you can live with? Miguel, is accepting his version of the call - accidental, if anything - something you can live with? Say it to each other, and then shake on it."
"Miguel, you started it with the bad call. Apologize first, and then we'll consider the shove. Nobody leaves until you do."
"This is going nowhere. I'll have the yard monitor suspend the handball game for the rest of the week, and that's the settlement."
"Darius, admit once and for all that your team probably saw it wrong - say that out loud right now so Miguel can hear it."
assets.theoretical_principle: Peer mediation with impartial phrasing and joint problem-solving: get each party to state and paraphrase the other's position, then engineer a mutually acceptable solution rather than a verdict from on high.
assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 0 follows the program's protocol - impartial framing, both positions stated and paraphrased, a solution both can live with, and a binding gesture (the agreement) that converts vindication into resolution. Choice 1 takes sides by demanding Miguel's apology first, destroying mediator impartiality; neither boy accepts a biased verdict. Choice 2 substitutes adult coercion for the concrete skills the program exists to teach, modeling that disputes are policed, not negotiated. Choice 3 forces a one-sided concession without hearing Miguel's side, manufacturing resentment that will resurface at the next recess.

assets.topic: The Feelings Roll Call: A Low Number
assets.visual_frame_description: Monday morning at the Nueva Learning Center. Fifteen fifth graders sit Indian-style in a circle on the hardwood floor of the old Crocker mansion. The teacher moves down the list calling names, and each child answers with a number from one (low spirits) to ten (high energy). Today Luke, his shoulders slumped and knees pulled in, answers "two." The circle falls quiet, and several pairs of eyes turn toward the teacher.
assets.player_mission: You are the teacher leading the opening circle. A low number is an invitation, never a demand: open the way for Luke to talk about what is troubling him, give the class the chance to air it as a topic of the day, and help the circle brainstorm creative options - without pressuring anyone to share.
key_concepts: Each Self Science class opens with a roll call in which students answer with a number indicating how they feel: one means low spirits, ten high energy.
When the numbers are low - ones, twos, or threes - it opens the way for someone to ask "Do you want to talk about why you feel that way?"
No one is pressured to talk about things they do not want to discuss.
Typical troubles in the lower grades are teasing, feeling left out, and fears.

Around sixth grade new concerns emerge: hurt feelings about not being asked on a date or being left out, immature friends, and the pressure of "My friends are smoking, and they're always trying to get me to try, too."
Such troubles are usually aired only on the periphery of school - at lunch, on the bus, at a friend's house - or kept to themselves, obsessing alone at night.
In Self Science these private troubles become "topics of the day," with the class considering creative options for handling them.
The explicit goal of Self Science is illuminating the child's sense of self and relationships with others.
Though the course has a lesson plan, it is flexible so that spontaneous moments can be capitalized on.
Karen Stone McCown: "Being emotionally literate is as important for learning as instruction in math and reading."
Self-awareness includes recognizing feelings and building a vocabulary for them, and seeing the links between thoughts, feelings, and reactions.

The first-grade "feelings cube" - rolling a cube with words such as sad or excited and describing a time you had that feeling - builds certainty in tying feelings to words and helps with empathy as children hear others having the same feelings.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the self-awareness check-in at the heart of Self Science: a numbered feelings roll call turns private, unspoken troubles into shared topics of the day, with the class brainstorming creative options while no one is forced to speak. Goleman describes the roll call as the curriculum's daily ritual for illuminating the child's sense of self and relationships, and for building a working vocabulary for feelings.

credibility.basis: Popular synthesis of affective research; EI construct scope debated

assets.scenario_setup: The roll call opened high today for the other students - "Ten, I'm jazzed, it's Friday" - but Luke answered "two." The rule of the circle is that a low number earns a gentle, optional invitation to talk. What happens in the next minute will decide whether Luke's science-fair worry becomes the day's lesson or gets buried.
dialogue: Varga (you): "Luke."
Luke (quietly): "Two."
Varga (you): "Do you want to talk about why you feel that way? No pressure - we can also just sit with it."
Luke: "The science-fair teams. They're picking partners this afternoon, and everybody's already pairing up. It's like I'm invisible."
Maya (a classmate, softly): "That's the worst. I got picked last at basketball once. I cried at home."
Luke (looking up): "You too? It's not just me?"
Varga (you): "Who else here has felt left out when teams were chosen?" (several hands go up)
Luke: "That actually helps. I didn't know anyone else felt that."
choices: Right - you're not alone, and that's exactly why we talk about this stuff in the circle. Let's take this as today's topic: what are some options for handling the pairing so you walk in prepared, no matter who picks you?
It's only Monday, Luke. Tomorrow's a new day. Let's move on so we can start the lesson.
I'll assign the pairs myself this afternoon, Luke, and make sure you're with someone friendly. Problem solved - you don't need to worry anymore.
A two is a serious number, Luke. You should go talk to the school counselor after class, and we'll keep the circle moving for now.
assets.theoretical_principle: The check-in as emotional self-awareness training: a low roll-call number opens a voluntary invitation to talk, the class airs the trouble as a topic of the day, and together they generate creative options rather than leaving the child to obsess alone.
assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 0 validates the feeling, mobilizes peer empathy (Luke discovers he is not alone), and converts a private worry into a group problem-solving exercise - the explicit design of the roll call and the flexible lesson plan. Choice 1 dismisses the disclosure, teaching that feelings are interruptions to the curriculum. Choice 2 removes Luke's agency: the curriculum's goal is that children learn options and assertiveness, not that adults quietly fix things for them. Choice 3 outs a normal, airable trouble to the counselor against the rule of no pressure, and pathologizes distress that the circle exists to hold.

assets.topic: Anger as a Secondary Reaction: Nia and Dani
assets.visual_frame_description: A Life Skills classroom at the Augusta Lewis Troup Middle School in New Haven, three times a week, mid-morning. Thirteen-year-old Nia sits with arms crossed and lips tight, having just announced that she will "never speak to Dani again." Dani, in the next four-desk cluster, stares hard at her notebook, cheeks flushed. The lesson today is identifying feelings and looking underneath them.
assets.player_mission: You are the teacher leading the class. Use the curriculum's rule about anger - it is almost always a secondary reaction - to help Nia find the primary feeling underneath (hurt, jealousy, fear of being left out), and help both girls convert the conflict into assertiveness and a workable solution, not a cold war.
key_concepts: Karen Stone McCown: "When we teach about anger, we help kids understand that it is almost always a secondary reaction and to look for what's underneath - are you hurt? jealous?"
Stone McCown: "Our kids learn that you always have choices about how you respond to emotion, and the more ways you know to respond to an emotion, the richer your life can be."
Managing emotions begins with realizing what is behind a feeling - for example, the hurt that triggers anger.
The curriculum teaches ways to handle anxieties, anger, and sadness rather than suppressing them.
Assertiveness - expressing feelings forthrightly in a way that will not spiral into aggression - is taught as distinct from both aggression and passivity.
Students learn to distinguish between what someone says or does and their own reactions and judgments.
The purpose of conflict resolution is to resolve disagreement and resentment before it spirals into an out-and-out fight.
Being able to name feelings, and so better distinguish between them, is a key emotional skill.
A girl once expelled from another school for fighting learned to approach an adversary and ask why she said those things rather than wading into an angry confrontation - a small but real victory.
Pooled evaluations show students in emotional-literacy courses gain better frustration tolerance and anger management, with fewer verbal put-downs, fights, and classroom disruptions.
Less aggressive and self-destructive behavior is a reported benefit of such programs.
Discussing what it feels like to be left out gives children the chance to try out new solutions - a corrective for the one-track thinking that sees conflict as the only route.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the curriculum's central rule about anger: anger is almost always a secondary reaction, so the coaching task is to find the primary feeling - the hurt or jealousy underneath - and express it assertively. Goleman presents Stone McCown's teaching that children who learn what is behind their anger, and the range of choices for responding, handle such conflicts without aggression.

credibility.basis: Popular synthesis of affective research; EI construct scope debated

assets.scenario_setup: Nia is furious because Dani - her best friend since third grade - chose two other girls for their group science project. Nia's stated plan is sarcastic digs at Dani "until she gets it." The class rule is that all feelings are okay; reactions differ. Your goal: get Nia to the feeling underneath and get both girls to a solution neither will regret at the science fair.
dialogue: Nia: "I don't care anymore. She can have her little project without me."
You: "Nia, we have a class rule about anger: it's almost always covering up another feeling. If you look underneath the mad - what's really there?"
Nia: "What do you mean? I'm just mad. She picked them over me."
You: "So is the underneath feeling hurt? Or jealous? Or scared you're losing your best friend?"
Nia (long pause, quieter): "Hurt. She's been my best friend since third grade. It feels like she replaced me."
Dani (looking up, stricken): "I didn't think it was like that. I thought you didn't want to work with me because I'm slow in science."
You: "See? Two different stories, same project. Nia, if you could tell Dani about the hurt - not the anger - what would you want her to hear?"
Nia: "That it felt like she dumped me. I just wanted her to ask me."
Dani: "I'm asking you now. Please be on my team."
choices: Nia, say to Dani what you just told me - about the hurt - and then let's brainstorm a project setup where you're both on the team and Dani still gets the help she wanted. Who has ideas?
Nia, angry words aren't okay in this class. The assignment is a letter to Dani apologizing for your outburst, due by the end of the period.
Nia, you're right to be mad - use it. Beat Dani's group at the science fair, and you'll feel great about it.
Nia, you need space. Take the rest of the period in the hallway to cool off, and no talking to Dani for a week so the anger doesn't flare again.
assets.theoretical_principle: Anger as secondary reaction with assertiveness training: coach the child to find the primary emotion underneath the anger (hurt at feeling replaced), express it forthrightly but without attack, and negotiate a creative compromise.
assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 0 does exactly what the curriculum prescribes: it names the underlying hurt, coaches its assertion without aggression, and generates a mutual solution - and it incidentally reveals Dani's own misread (fear that Nia thought her slow). Choice 1 punishes the anger itself and demands a forced apology before the hurt is even processed; the resentment simply goes underground. Choice 2 deliberately inflames the secondary reaction and models aggression as a coping tool. Choice 3 isolates Nia in the exact "clamming up" pattern the course teaches against, leaving the rift to fester into the science fair and beyond.

assets.topic: Emotional Literacy in Disguise: The Math-Class Moment
assets.visual_frame_description: A fifth-grade math classroom in a school running the Child Development Project. Ten o'clock, and the timed multiplication drill is about to start, but Marcus is staring out the window replaying lunch, Lena is rummaging frantically through her backpack, and two boys are still talking over their desks. There is no separate feelings class here; the emotional lesson is woven into the math period itself.
assets.player_mission: You are Mr. Osei, the teacher. Use the misbehavior and distraction in the room as a disguised study-skills lesson: name the distractions, model self-talk, and teach impulse management and self-motivation so the class can actually attend to the drill - and take the skill with them.
key_concepts: An emerging strategy in emotional education is not to create a new class but to blend lessons on feelings and relationships with other subjects already taught.

Some emotional-learning lessons are taught as part of math class - notably basic study skills such as how to put aside distractions, motivate yourself to study, and manage your impulses so you can attend to learning.
The Child Development Project, directed by Eric Schaps in Oakland, California, infiltrates social and emotional lessons into the very fabric of school life instead of taking separate class time.
In the project, first graders in reading class get "Frog and Toad Are Friends" as a platform for discussing friendship and how people feel when someone plays a trick on them.
Misbehavior is treated as a ripe opportunity to teach skills that are lacking - impulse control, explaining feelings, resolving conflicts - with better ways to discipline than coercion.
When three first graders push to be first in the lunch line, the teacher may suggest each guess a number and let the winner go first: an impartial, fair way to settle a pint-size dispute.
The deeper teaching of such moments is that disputes can be negotiated - an approach children can carry to settle other disputes in one form or another through much of life.
Children who lack impulse control have special trouble paying attention to what is being taught and so fall behind in their learning and grades.
Pooled program evaluations show students become less impulsive, are better able to focus on the task at hand, and show improved self-control.
Emotional literacy programs improve academic achievement scores - a finding that recurs again and again in such studies.
The emotional-literacy movement educates affect itself, whereas the affective-education movement of the 1960s used affect to educate.
Emotional literacy goes hand in hand with education for character, for moral development, and for citizenship - values children need to practice, not just be lectured about.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests emotional literacy in disguise: skills such as putting aside distractions, motivating yourself, and managing impulses are taught inside standard subjects like math, because children who cannot manage impulses fall behind academically. Goleman reports that blended approaches like the Child Development Project treat misbehavior as a teachable moment and that pooled evaluations show both better self-control and improved achievement scores.

credibility.basis: Popular synthesis of affective research; EI construct scope debated

assets.scenario_setup: The drill starts in ninety seconds, and the class is not ready. Punishing the distractions would end the moment; ignoring them would surrender it. Your goal is to turn the universal experience of a wandering mind into the real lesson of the period - attention as a skill - while still getting the class to the drill.
dialogue: Mr. Osei (you): "Before the drill - a sixty-second check-in. Right now, what is pulling your attention away from the math?"
Marcus: "The basketball game at lunch. I keep replaying the last shot."
Lena: "I left my worksheet at home and I'm already panicking about the grade."
Mr. Osei (you): "Good - naming the distraction is step one. Marcus, what is one thing you can do with that replay until lunch?"
Marcus: "Tell myself it's coming anyway? It's not going anywhere. I can see it at noon."
Mr. Osei (you): "Exactly - that's self-talk working. Lena, what would you tell a friend who forgot a worksheet?"
Lena (thinking): "That the teacher knows it happens sometimes, and to do today's work and bring tomorrow's assignment."
Mr. Osei (you): "Then say that to yourself. Panic and focus cannot share the same desk."
choices: Right. Now before we begin, everyone silently names one impulse they're setting aside for the next fifteen minutes - the talking, the replay, the worry - and then we work. That naming is the skill; the drill is the practice.
Good talk, everyone. Lena, five points off for the missing homework; Marcus, eyes on the board. Begin the drill now.
You know what - the drill can wait. Everyone push your desks together; we're doing a feelings circle instead. Math is tomorrow.
Marcus and Lena, since you were both distracted, you'll both stay at recess to finish the drill with me. Start writing your corrections now.
assets.theoretical_principle: Embedded emotional learning: teach attention, impulse management, and self-motivation explicitly inside the academic lesson, because competence in these skills is what makes the academic work possible.
assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 0 converts the moment into a transferable skill - naming distractions, applying self-talk, and deliberately setting an impulse aside - which is precisely the study-skills content the book says belongs inside math class, and it keeps the drill intact. Choice 1 punishes the exact impulse-control failures the moment was meant to train, teaching compliance rather than competence. Choice 2 abandons the academic content, defeating the "disguise": the point is that the subject and the skill are taught in the same period. Choice 3 turns a lapse into detention, modeling that feelings are a nuisance adults must police rather than a capacity children can build.

assets.topic: Multiple Perspectives: The Jeep at the Pizza Shop
assets.visual_frame_description: A ninth-grade social development class in a New Haven high school. Marcus, fifteen, slams his notebook onto his desk, face flushed, after describing what he saw at the pizza shop: his girlfriend, Aaliyah, laughing and leaning in close with another boy, Malik. He is halfway out of his seat to "go find out what that's about" - a confrontation he frames as self-respect.
assets.player_mission: You are the teacher. Before Marcus plunges into a confrontation, coach the ninth-grade skill of multiple perspectives: have him generate what Malik and Aaliyah might be experiencing from their points of view, weigh what a hot approach would actually cost him, and convert the impulse into a clarifying, assertive conversation.
key_concepts: By ninth grade the New Haven curriculum emphasizes the ability to take multiple perspectives - your own as well as those of others involved.

A New Haven teacher's example: a kid who is mad because he saw his girlfriend talking with another guy is encouraged to consider what might be going on from their point of view, too, rather than just plunge into a confrontation.
Conflict begins with not communicating, making assumptions, and jumping to conclusions.
Most adolescents are ten to fifteen years old when they are exposed to sexuality, alcohol and drugs, and smoking - the pressures that sixth-grade lessons begin to address.
Students who have had emotional literacy classes find the new pressures of peer politics less troubling than their peers do.
Empathy - understanding others' feelings and taking their perspective, and respecting differences in how people feel - is a key social ability.
Seeing things from another's perspective breaks down biased stereotypes, and so breeds tolerance and acceptance of differences.
David Hamburg lists an optimistic outlook, postponing gratification, social responsibility in appropriate ways, and maintaining control over one's emotions as essentials for profiting from school.
Emotional literacy programs help children better fulfill their roles in life - becoming better friends, students, and eventually husbands, wives, workers, and citizens.
Tim Shriver's verdict: "A rising tide lifts all boats. It's not just the kids with problems, but all kids who can benefit from these skills; these are an inoculation for life."
The transition to middle school and then high school brings a dip in self-confidence and a jump in self-consciousness, making peer confrontations especially loaded.

The SOCS method - Situation, Options, Consequences, Solutions - offers a grown-up version of the stoplight for real-life decisions, loved by Lamont for handling problems with girlfriends and avoiding fights.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests perspective-taking, the ninth-grade capstone skill of the New Haven curriculum: before acting on a perceived slight, generate the other people's points of view and question the assumption that what you saw means what it seems. Goleman reports that this training is what helps adolescents handle ambiguous social realities without plunging into confrontations.

credibility.basis: Popular synthesis of affective research; EI construct scope debated

assets.scenario_setup: Marcus is convinced he has been wronged and his standing among the guys is at stake; he wants to go now and "settle it." His account contains a usable seed - Malik is in Aaliyah's history class, and she mentioned a study group last week - but Marcus has not connected it. Your goal is to slow the impulse into perspective and a plan, without ever denying his feelings.
dialogue: Marcus: "I saw her with Malik. Laughing, leaned in close, at the pizza shop. I'm going over there right now."
You: "Marcus, before you go anywhere - walk me through what Malik and Aaliyah might be experiencing right now. Give me two or three possibilities."
Marcus: "What do you mean, possibilities? It's obvious what was happening."
You: "Obvious is one story. Are there others? Could Malik be a cousin? A study partner for the history midterm? Someone she's helping?"
Marcus (pausing): "He... is in her history class. She said something about a study group last week."
You: "And if you walk in hot - even if you're completely right - what do you actually get?"
Marcus: "A fight, maybe. Or her thinking I don't trust her. Probably both."
You: "So what do you want instead? And what would you have to do to get it?"
Marcus: "I want to know the truth without wrecking us. So I guess... talk to her tonight, calm."
choices: Good. So tonight, not in front of the guys: "I saw you with Malik and my head went somewhere bad. What was that about?" - and then listen. If it's a study group, you've lost nothing; if it's not, you've lost nothing either. Tell me how you'd handle her answer if it's the bad one.
Fine, then, but you need to go NOW, Marcus. Waiting makes you look like a coward - a real man finds out for himself, tonight, on the spot.
This is serious enough that I'm calling Aaliyah's parents, Marcus. That kind of stalking energy is something the school needs to document before it gets worse.
Honestly, Marcus, the cleanest move is to break up with her by text right now and never look back. You keep your dignity, and you can't be played.
assets.theoretical_principle: Multiple perspectives before action: delay the angry impulse by generating the other parties' points of view, examine assumptions, then act assertively - a confrontation only after information, not instead of it.
assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 0 keeps the lesson alive: after perspective generation, Marcus converts rage into an assertive, information-gathering conversation with a fallback plan - the exact coaching the New Haven ninth-grade teacher describes. Choice 1 inflames the impulse and welds aggression to masculinity, which is precisely the escalation path the program exists to interrupt. Choice 2 catastrophizes ordinary jealousy into institutional action against Aaliyah, robbing Marcus of agency and modeling that feelings must be reported, not managed. Choice 3 collapses the relationship on an unverified assumption - the "jumping to conclusions" that starts conflicts and, in less privileged settings than this classroom, ends them in hallway shootings.

assets.topic: The Cooperation Squares: Silence and the Gestalt
assets.visual_frame_description: In Jo-An Varga's fifth-grade Self Science class, three groups sit at three tables, each racing to assemble square-shaped jigsaw puzzles in total silence, with no gesturing allowed. Three observers, each familiar with the game, hold evaluation sheets. Table A is done. Table B slowly merged from separate efforts into a unit. Table C - Sean, Fairlie, and Rahman - is stuck on a puzzle that looks more like a trapezoid than a square, with three frustrated children scanning and seizing pieces that never fit.
assets.player_mission: You are studying the cooperation dynamics the game exposes. First, diagnose why Table C is failing while Table B succeeded. Then, in the escalated moment, choose the intervention that unlocks the team without doing its work for it.
key_concepts: In the Cooperation Squares game, teams must assemble square-shaped jigsaw puzzles in silence, with no gesturing allowed.
Three observers, each familiar with the game, rate who takes the lead in organizing, who is a clown, and who disrupts.
One group finished in just a few minutes because its members coordinated effortlessly as a unit.
A second group first engaged in solitary, parallel efforts - each working separately on their own puzzle - and got nowhere until they slowly started to work collectively.
The struggling third group had only one puzzle nearing completion, and even that looked more like a trapezoid than a square.
Rahman broke the tension by holding two puzzle pieces up over his eyes like a mask, making his partners giggle - a pivotal moment in the day's lesson.
Varga's instruction - "Those of you who have finished can give one specific hint to those who are still working" - structured help so the struggling team still did its own work.
Dagan pointed to two pieces that jutted out from the square and said, "You've got to move those two pieces around."
Rahman suddenly grasped the new gestalt, and the pieces quickly fell into place - first one puzzle, then the others, to spontaneous applause.
Cooperation in this game means seeing the whole puzzle, not just the pieces in front of you - the skill that distinguished the tables.
Emotional lessons delivered regularly and repeated over years become strengthened neural pathways, habits applied in times of duress, frustration, and hurt.
Like good childrearing, the lessons of these classes are small but telling, delivered regularly over a sustained period.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests cooperative problem-solving under a communication constraint: silence and no gestures, so success depends on perceiving teammates' needs and offering the right piece at the right moment. Goleman uses the Cooperation Squares game at Nueva to show how coordination itself - not individual puzzle skill - determined which team succeeded, and how a single specific hint unlocked a new gestalt.

credibility.basis: Popular synthesis of affective research; EI construct scope debated

assets.boss_battle_explanation: Cooperation Squares strips away words and gestures, forcing a team to coordinate purely by reading each other's moves and needs. The game's object lesson is that smooth coordination - treating the pieces as a shared pool and sensing what teammates still require - beats solitary cleverness, and that a well-timed, specific piece of help lets a stuck team discover the solution itself.
assets.stage_1_observation: Three groups race to assemble their squares in silence. Table A finished in minutes. Table B started with four members each working separately on their own puzzle, getting nowhere, then slowly shifted to building one square together as a unit until all were solved. Table C still struggles, with only one nearly-complete puzzle that looks more like a trapezoid than a square; Sean, Fairlie, and Rahman are frantically scanning the table, seizing on likely possibilities, and placing pieces near partly finished squares only to be disappointed by the lack of fit.
assets.stage_1_question: What best explains why Table C is stuck while Table B eventually succeeded?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Table B succeeded because its members shifted from solitary, parallel efforts to working collectively as a unit, while Table C never achieved that smooth coordination: each member kept pursuing his or her own partial square, so no one was tracking the pieces their teammates actually needed - the hallmark of the game is seeing the group's puzzles as one shared whole.
assets.stage_2_intervention: The tension breaks when Rahman holds two pieces over his eyes like a mask. Varga announces: "Those of you who have finished can give one specific hint to those who are still working." Dagan approaches the struggling table, points to two pieces that jut out from the square, and says, "You've got to move those two pieces around." Suddenly Rahman's furrowed face clears, and the pieces fall into place, first on one puzzle, then the others, to spontaneous applause. Which quality made this intervention the pivotal one?
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: The hint was minimal, specific, and non-judgmental: it identified exactly which two pieces to move without assembling anything for them, preserving the team's role - and because the constraint of silence prevented gesture, the verbal pointer let Rahman grasp the new gestalt himself, making the discovery the team's own and the lesson a memorable one.

assets.topic: Reading Emotions from Faces: Ekman's Recipes
assets.visual_frame_description: In Joyce Andrews's fifth-grade Life Skills class at Troup Middle School, New Haven, the eighteen students who made it to school sit in four-desk clusters, hands straining high. On the board is a list of feelings - sadness, worry, excitement, frustration, aggravated. On each desk lies a mimeographed worksheet: faces of boys and girls displaying the six basic emotions, each paired with a description of the facial-muscle activity beneath it.
assets.player_mission: You are mastering the lesson that comes straight from Paul Ekman's research: connect the name of a feeling, the feeling itself, and the facial expression that matches it. Use the recipes to identify the emotion on a face, then apply the same skill to a live confrontation before anyone acts on a misread.
key_concepts: The facial-expression lesson at Troup comes straight from Paul Ekman's research; it is taught in most college introductory psychology courses and rarely, if ever, in grade school.
The six basic emotions taught are happy, sad, angry, surprised, afraid, and disgusted.

The worksheet pairs each emotion with the facial-muscle activity underlying it; the recipe for afraid: the mouth is open and drawn back, the eyes are open with the inner corners going up, the eyebrows are raised and drawn together, and there are wrinkles in the middle of the forehead.
Being able to name feelings, and so better distinguish between them, is a key emotional skill.
Students were assigned to bring in magazine pictures of a person's face, name the emotion the face displays, and explain how to tell the person has those feelings.
Schoolyard bullies often strike out in anger because they misinterpret neutral messages and expressions as hostile.
Girls who develop eating disorders fail to distinguish anger from anxiety from hunger - a common lapse in just this kind of emotional literacy.
The Life Skills class on reading emotions from facial expressions is essentially about empathizing.
The PATHS curriculum teaches children to recognize when someone is actually hostile, as opposed to when the attribution of hostility comes from oneself.
Expressions float over the kids' faces as they imitate the pictures and follow the facial-muscle recipes - practice that makes the naming automatic.
Emotional self-awareness - recognizing feelings and building a vocabulary for them - is the keystone topic of the curriculum.
Empathy, understanding others' feelings and taking their perspective, is a key social ability built on reading such cues.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests a core emotional-literacy skill: naming a feeling by matching it to the specific facial-muscle configuration it produces, per Ekman's research on facial expression. Goleman argues that this elementary lesson is an antidote to common lapses - bullies who strike out because they misread neutral faces as hostile, or girls who cannot tell anger from anxiety from hunger.

credibility.basis: Popular synthesis of affective research; EI construct scope debated

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The worksheet gives each of the six basic emotions a recipe of facial-muscle activity, and the class follows the recipes in front of a mirror of their own faces. Mastery means a face is no longer an impression but a pattern you can read - and, critically, that you can check your own projection against the recipe before acting.
assets.stage_1_observation: A new face is displayed: the mouth is open and drawn back, the eyes are open and the inner corners go up, the eyebrows are raised and drawn together, and there are wrinkles in the middle of the forehead. The class reads the recipe aloud, imitating it, and expressions of fear, anger, surprise, or disgust float over their faces as they try each one.
assets.stage_1_question: According to the worksheet's facial-muscle recipe, which of the six basic emotions does this configuration signal?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Afraid: the mouth is open and drawn back; the eyes are open with the inner corners going up; the eyebrows are raised and drawn together; and there are wrinkles in the middle of the forehead - this distinctive combination is the recipe for fear, not anger (brows lowered and pulled together, lips pressed) and not surprise (eyes wide, brows high but not drawn together).
assets.stage_2_intervention: That afternoon in the cafeteria, a classmate claims another boy "gave him a look that meant fight" - a flat, neutral face glimpsed over a lunch tray - and is already spoiling to confront him. The teacher calls on the class to apply the morning's lesson. What is the correct application before anyone so much as stands up?
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Check the claimed threat against the recipes first: a flat, neutral face matches no hostile configuration, so the hostility is coming from the observer's projection, not the display - the exact pattern in which schoolyard bullies misread neutral messages and expressions as hostile and lash out; the skill is to recognize when someone is actually hostile versus when the attribution comes from oneself.

assets.topic: The Stoplight: Impulse Control Step by Step
assets.visual_frame_description: A fourth-grade New Haven classroom with the stoplight poster displayed prominently on the wall: RED LIGHT - stop, calm down, and think before you act; YELLOW LIGHT - say the problem and how you feel; set a positive goal; think of lots of solutions; think ahead to the consequences; GREEN LIGHT - go ahead and try the best plan. On the rug, Marcus stands fists clenched, face reddening, after being teased about his new short haircut.
assets.player_mission: You are coaching Marcus through the six steps at the moment he is about to strike out. The stoplight is invoked exactly when a child is about to hit, withdraw into a huff, or burst into tears - your job is to walk him through the sequence in the correct order so the impulse passes through thought on its way to action.
key_concepts: The stoplight poster has six steps: red light - stop, calm down, and think before you act.
The yellow light continues: say the problem and how you feel; set a positive goal; think of lots of solutions; think ahead to the consequences.
The green light step: go ahead and try the best plan.
The stoplight is regularly invoked when a child is about to strike out in anger, withdraw into a huff at some slight, or burst into tears at being teased.
Beyond the management of feelings, the stoplight points a way to more effective action.
As a habitual way of thinking before acting from feelings, the stoplight can evolve into a basic strategy for dealing with the risks of adolescence and beyond.
The same stoplight exercise is used in the New Haven courses and in the PATHS curriculum as a tool for teaching self-control.
The premise children learn about anger: "all feelings are okay to have," but some reactions are okay and others not.
Fourth- and fifth-grade lessons focus on empathy, impulse control, and anger management, as peer relationships take on immense importance.
A girl once expelled from another school for fighting later applied exactly this training: she approached her would-be adversary and asked why she said those things instead of attacking first.
Pooled evaluations show students in such programs are less impulsive and better able to express anger appropriately without fighting.
Children who lack the ability to control impulses have special trouble paying attention and fall behind in their learning and grades.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the stoplight method of impulse control: a concrete six-step sequence that converts a charged moment - about to hit, withdraw, or cry - into a pause, a problem statement, and a chosen plan. Goleman reports the stoplight is the shared self-control tool of the New Haven program and PATHS, one that can become a lifelong strategy for acting instead of erupting.

credibility.basis: Popular synthesis of affective research; EI construct scope debated

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The stoplight gives children a physical, repeatable sequence to run at the peak of an impulse: red to stop and calm, yellow to name the problem, set a goal, brainstorm solutions, and weigh consequences, green to act on the chosen plan. Mastery is running the sequence in order when the body is hot, not remembering it in the abstract.
assets.stage_1_observation: Marcus has just been teased - "bald beanie!" - and the class watches him stand up, fists clenched, face going red, about to shove the teaser. The teacher catches his eye, taps the stoplight poster on the wall, and asks Marcus to talk the sequence through before any muscle moves. Marcus is breathing hard, and the room is silent.
assets.stage_1_question: Under the red light, what is the single first step Marcus must take?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Stop, calm down, and think before you act - the red light contains exactly this instruction, and it comes first, before naming the problem, before goals, before solutions; without the calm, every later step is run by the hot amygdala.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Marcus has stopped, turned away, exhaled hard, and reported: "Jalen teased me about my haircut and I feel humiliated - I want to shove him." He has stated the problem and his feeling and set a positive goal: "Leave this afternoon without a fight." Now he is working the yellow light: solution one - "tell Jalen it's my haircut and I don't like the joke"; solution two - "ignore him and walk to the water fountain"; solution three - "shove him once and say that's for the haircut." What is the remaining yellow-light step he must complete before green?
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Think ahead to the consequences of each solution - the shove earns a suspension under the school's unbeatable rule against fighting, the direct words risk an escalation, the walk to the fountain ends the incident - and only then, on the green light, go ahead and try the best plan.

assets.topic: The Emotional Timetable: Sequencing the Lessons
assets.visual_frame_description: A district planning room where a social-emotional curriculum committee maps lessons onto grades. Charts line the walls: the feelings cube for first grade, the stoplight and anger management for fourth and fifth, temptations of sex, drugs, and drinking for sixth, multiple perspectives for ninth, and a highlighted note that the kindergarten year is the peak ripening of the "social emotions." A parent's letter sits on the table complaining that her four-year-old son brags constantly and must be "taught humility."
assets.player_mission: You are the curriculum advisor. Judge whether the parent's complaint fits the child's emotional timetable, then rule on two scheduling proposals against what developmental psychology - as Goleman presents it - says about when each lesson belongs.
key_concepts: Adults all too readily fall into the trap of expecting children to have reached a maturity far beyond their years, forgetting that each emotion has its preprogrammed moment of appearance in a child's growth.
The self-consciousness that can breed humility typically does not emerge until around age five, so a four-year-old's braggadocio is age-typical, not a character flaw.

The kindergarten year marks a peak ripening of the "social emotions" - insecurity and humility, jealousy and envy, pride and confidence - all of which require the capacity to compare oneself with others.

David Hamburg on ages six to eleven: "school is a crucible and a defining experience that will heavily influence children's adolescence and beyond," where a child's sense of self-worth depends substantially on achievement.
The transition to middle school brings a dip in self-confidence, a jump in self-consciousness, and one of the greatest blows: "social self-esteem," confidence that one can make and keep friends.
Hamburg: "most adolescents are ten to fifteen years old when they are exposed to sexuality, alcohol and drugs, smoking" - which is why sixth-grade lessons address those temptations.
In first grade students roll the "feelings cube," with words such as sad or excited, and describe a time they had that feeling.
Fourth- and fifth-grade lessons target empathy, impulse control, and anger management as peer relationships take on immense importance.
In sixth grade the lessons relate directly to the temptations and pressures for sex, drugs, or drinking that begin to enter children's lives.
By ninth grade, students confront more ambiguous social realities, and the ability to take multiple perspectives - your own as well as those of others involved - is emphasized.
T. Berry Brazelton proposes coaching parents as emotional mentors to infants and toddlers, as some home-visit programs do.
Well-run Head Start programs can have beneficial long-term emotional and social effects into early adulthood - fewer drug problems and arrests, better marriages, greater earning power.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the emotional timetable: lessons must be pegged to the child's development because each emotion has a preprogrammed moment of appearance tied to cognitive and biological maturation. Goleman argues that interventions work best when they track this timetable - kindergarten for the social emotions, the middle-school transition for friendship skills, sixth grade for the temptations that actually begin at ten to fifteen.

credibility.basis: Popular synthesis of affective research; EI construct scope debated

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The emotional timetable is the map of when each competence can actually take root: the social-comparison emotions peak in kindergarten, school achievement shapes self-worth from six to eleven, self-confidence dips and social self-esteem is wounded at the middle-school transition, and sexuality, alcohol, drugs, and smoking press on children from about ten to fifteen. Reading the timetable correctly means neither expecting too much too early nor scheduling a lesson after its window.
assets.stage_1_observation: A parent writes in: her four-year-old brags endlessly - about his tower, his drawing, his speed - and she wants him disciplined hard for "conceit and vanity" before it becomes arrogance. The committee members are divided: several parents agree with her; one developmental psychologist on the team cites the research on when self-consciousness emerges.
assets.stage_1_question: How should the committee advise the parent, given the emotional timetable?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Not to punish the boasting as conceit: the self-consciousness that can breed humility typically does not emerge until around age five, so a four-year-old's braggadocio is an age-typical display rather than early arrogance - and reprimanding it fights the timetable instead of working with it.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Two scheduling proposals reach the committee. Proposal A: pull the sixth-grade temptation lessons (sex, drugs, drinking, smoking) down to third grade, because "kids these days know everything early." Proposal B: move the kindergarten social-comparison work (inclusion, envy, pride, jealousy) up to seventh grade, where the middle-school self-confidence dip makes it clearly relevant. The chair asks you to rule.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Reject both: the temptation lessons belong at sixth grade because most adolescents are ten to fifteen when they are actually exposed to sexuality, alcohol and drugs, and smoking - teaching them earlier detaches the lesson from the risk; and the social-comparison work keeps its strongest place in kindergarten, where the social emotions peak, because the middle-school transition - with its dip in self-confidence and blow to social self-esteem - is exactly when the curriculum should be buttressing friendship-building skills and self-confidence, not starting social-comparison lessons late.

assets.topic: The Misread Face: Hostility That Was Never There
assets.visual_frame_description: A New Haven schoolyard at 11:52 on a Tuesday morning, captured in a time-stamped observation log. Fifth grader Devon has just shoved schoolmate Sam, who was kneeling at the fence tying his shoe. A teacher separates them as Devon, red-faced, shouts that Sam "gave him the look." The class completed the Ekman facial-expression lesson two weeks ago; Devon's was the one desk without the worksheet completed.
assets.player_mission: You are auditing the incident for the school's social-development team. Compare Devon's baseline behavior, the timed nonverbal log, and the interrogation transcript, then diagnose what actually triggered the shove - and whether the facial-expression training Devon missed would have changed it.
key_concepts: Schoolyard bullies often strike out in anger because they misinterpret neutral messages and expressions as hostile.
The facial-expression lesson - from Paul Ekman's research - maps each of the six basic emotions to a recipe of facial-muscle activity.
The recipe for afraid: mouth open and drawn back, eyes open with inner corners up, eyebrows raised and drawn together, wrinkles in the middle of the forehead.
The PATHS curriculum teaches children, especially those prone to aggression, how to recognize when someone is actually hostile as opposed to when the attribution of hostility comes from oneself.
The Life Skills class on reading emotions from facial expressions is essentially about empathizing.
Empathy - understanding others' feelings and taking their perspective - builds on self-awareness.
Conflict typically escalates from not communicating, making assumptions, and jumping to conclusions.

The stoplight method (stop, calm down, think; say the problem and how you feel; set a positive goal; think of lots of solutions; think ahead to consequences; go ahead and try the best plan) is invoked when a child is about to strike out in anger.
Pooled evaluations of emotional-literacy programs show fewer fights and verbal put-downs among students who take them.
Children who lack these lessons "just aren't very good at avoiding disputes."
All feelings are okay to have, but some reactions are okay and others not.
Awareness of one's own triggers - and the ability to check a hostile read against the evidence of the other's face - is a core competence taught from the earliest school years.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests misattributed hostility: a child reads a neutral face as a threat and strikes out on the strength of his own projection. Goleman reports that bullies typically misinterpret neutral messages and expressions as hostile, which is precisely why schools teach Ekman's facial recipes and why PATHS drills the distinction between actual hostility and hostility attributed from within.

credibility.basis: Popular synthesis of affective research; EI construct scope debated

assets.question: Given Devon's baseline and the observation log, what does his shove of Sam reveal about the trigger?
assets.subject_baseline: Devon is a quick-tempered fifth grader with a documented pattern of "striking out first": he reads neutral glances, flat tones, and ordinary jostles as deliberate insults and attacks before asking anything. Teachers note he returned the facial-expression worksheet blank, skipped the imitation practice, and excused his earlier outbursts with "he looked at me funny."
observed_nonverbal_log: 11:52:00 - Sam kneels at the fence to retie his shoe; as Devon's group passes, Sam's head turns toward Devon while his face stays flat and neutral throughout.
11:52:07 - Devon stops abruptly; his eyebrows pull down into a glare; his fists clench and his posture squares; he says nothing.
11:52:11 - Devon's jaw clenches; without any provocation from Sam his voice rises: "What!"
11:52:14 - Sam, surprised by the shout, opens his mouth slightly and raises his eyebrows - the surprise configuration, not a hostile one - and says "Nothing, bro."
11:52:16 - Devon shoves Sam, shouting "Don't look at me like that!"
11:52:20 - After a teacher separates them, Devon's body relaxes quickly; he insists Sam "gave him the face," but he cannot imitate any expression Sam actually made.
interrogation_transcript: Teacher: "Devon, what did Sam actually do before you pushed him?"
Devon: "He looked at me. You know - that look. Like he wanted to start something."
Teacher: "Show me the look with your own face, please." (Devon produces an exaggerated sneer that matches no basic-emotion recipe.)
Teacher: "Sam says he was tying his shoe and just glanced up because he heard your group coming. Could that be the whole thing?"
Devon (long pause): "Maybe. I don't know. It felt like a challenge."
Teacher: "Felt like - or was? What in the facial recipe said hostile?"
Devon: "Nothing, I guess. I just didn't like it."
assets.correct_diagnosis: Devon lashed out because he misread a neutral glance as a hostile challenge: the anger and the threat both came from Devon's own attribution, not from anything Sam's face displayed.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: Every log entry contradicts Devon's story: Sam's face stays flat from 11:52:00 to 11:52:07, and his only motion before the shove is the surprise configuration - open mouth, raised eyebrows - which matches no hostile recipe. Devon's testimony collapses under questioning ("Maybe. I don't know. It felt like a challenge"), and he cannot reproduce an expression Sam actually made. This is precisely the pattern Goleman describes: schoolyard bullies often strike out in anger because they misinterpret neutral messages and expressions as hostile - the failure the Ekman-based lesson treats, and the target of PATHS' distinction between someone actually hostile and hostility attributed from oneself. Devon skipped that exact lesson, and his "striking out first" baseline shows the missing competence: checking a hostile read against the evidence of the other's face.
distractors: Sam deliberately provoked Devon with a subtle sneer that he is skilled enough to hide from the observation log and the teacher.
Devon's shove proves he is a psychopath who feels no empathy and will attack anyone regardless of their expression.
Devon reacted correctly: in a tense schoolyard, any glance from a non-group member is a real threat signal, and the shove was proportionate self-defense.

assets.topic: The Hidden Hurt Behind the Outburst
assets.visual_frame_description: A Self Science observation session at the Nueva Learning Center, logged over one March morning. Seven-year-old Kalil, normally cheerful and cooperative, has spent three days short-tempered: refusing eye contact in the circle, sighing loudly, and this morning erupting at teammates during the Cooperation Squares game when a piece would not fit. The timed log and interview transcript below are what the school's facilitator reviews to decide what is really going on with him.
assets.player_mission: You are the facilitator auditing this incident. Weigh the baseline, the timed nonverbal log, and the transcript, then diagnose the true driver of Kalil's outbursts - and what coaching he needs next.
key_concepts: Karen Stone McCown's teaching: anger is almost always a secondary reaction - children are coached to look for what is underneath: hurt, jealousy, or being left out.
Managing emotions begins with realizing what is behind a feeling - for example, the hurt that triggers anger.
The troubles of childhood - teasing, feeling left out, fears - are usually aired only on the periphery of school, if at all, and are often kept to themselves, obsessing about them alone at night.
Low feelings roll-call numbers open the way for someone to ask "Do you want to talk about why you feel that way?", with no one pressured to speak.
Conflict typically escalates from not communicating, making assumptions, and jumping to conclusions, and from sending a "hard" message that makes it tough to hear what you are saying.
The point of conflict resolution is not to avoid conflict but to resolve the disagreement and resentment before it spirals into an out-and-out fight.
Assertiveness - expressing feelings forthrightly in a way that will not spiral into aggression - is distinct from aggression and passivity.
Mastery in the emotional domain is difficult because skills must be acquired when people are least able to take in new information: when they are upset.
"Anyone, adult or fifth grader, needs some help being a self-observer when they're so upset," says Varga - the coaching itself is the lesson.
What could have been the seed of a full-fledged battle can instead heighten mastery of the nuances of conflict resolution.
Emotional lessons delivered regularly, over years, become strengthened neural pathways applied in times of duress, frustration, and hurt.
The purpose of the flexible lesson plan is to capitalize on spontaneous moments when children bring up issues.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests anger as a secondary reaction: surface outbursts at a trivial trigger mask a primary emotion - hurt at being left out - that the child cannot name without coaching. Goleman presents this as the core managing-emotions lesson of the Self Science curriculum, which drills children to look for the hurt underneath the anger.

credibility.basis: Popular synthesis of affective research; EI construct scope debated

assets.question: Given Kalil's baseline and the logged morning, what is the correct diagnosis of his outbursts?
assets.subject_baseline: Kalil is a normally cheerful, cooperative seven-year-old who joins the feelings circle easily and has never had a documented outburst. Since Tuesday - the day the class openly discussed Mateo's birthday party, which Kalil was not invited to - he has been irritable: short answers, refusal of eye contact, loud sighs during circle, and a low feelings number this morning.
observed_nonverbal_log: 09:15 - Circle roll call. Kalil answers "three" - a low number - but when asked "Do you want to talk about why?" he shrugs, looks at the floor, and says "I'm fine."
09:18 - As another boy recounts the party ("Mateo's party was so fun"), Kalil's jaw tightens, his arms cross, and his lower lip pulls in; he looks away.
09:41 - During Cooperation Squares, Kalil grabs a puzzle piece from Tamika's hand without asking; when she objects, his voice escalates: "You're all stupid!"
09:44 - After the teacher separates him, Kalil's shoulders slump and he blinks rapidly; he mutters, "It's not about the stupid game."
09:46 - With the teacher sitting beside him, Kalil's voice drops and his eyes well up: "Nobody invited me to the party. They all got to go."
interrogation_transcript: Teacher: "The game made you so angry. What was going on inside?"
Kalil: "I don't know. I just wanted them to stop."
Teacher: "This morning in the circle you answered three, then said, 'I'm fine.' Was that the whole truth?"
Kalil (tears welling): "Mateo's party. Everybody went. I wasn't invited."
Teacher: "So the anger at the game - was that anger really about the puzzle?"
Kalil: "I guess. I felt left out. And I didn't want anyone to see."
assets.correct_diagnosis: Kalil's outbursts were anger as a secondary reaction: the surface rage at the puzzle and his classmates masked the primary feeling - hurt at being left out of Mateo's party - which he could not name until coached to look underneath.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: The log shows the exact sequence the curriculum predicts: a hurtful event (exclusion from the party), mounting irritability, a low roll-call number denied with a false "I'm fine," an outbreak at a trivial trigger (the grabbed piece), and - once the teacher sat beside him - the primary emotion surfacing in Kalil's own words: "I felt left out. And I didn't want anyone to see." That self-imposed silence matches the book's observation that children obsess over such troubles alone and never air them. The truthful baseline, the anger-at-trivia pattern, and the revealed hurt together confirm Stone McCown's rule - anger is almost always a secondary reaction - and point to the right coaching: name the buried feeling and practice assertive expression rather than punishing the outburst.
distractors: Kalil is a naturally aggressive child: the snatching and name-calling prove a dispositional trait that no curriculum can change.
Kalil's "I'm fine" was the truth: the game frustrated him, the moment passed, and the party is a separate matter he will forget by Friday.
Kalil is manipulating the teacher: the low number, the tight jaw, and the tears are performed to become the center of the circle.
